title: A Single Population Mean using the Normal Distribution

slides.title: The target parameter
slides.body: A confidence interval for a population mean estimates μ.
slides.question: For transfer duration, does μ describe one transfer, the sample mean, or the population mean?

slides.title: A point estimate
slides.body: A point estimate uses one sample statistic to estimate a population parameter.
slides.question: Which statistic estimates the population mean transfer duration?

slides.title: An interval estimate
slides.body: An interval estimate gives a range of plausible values for a population parameter.
slides.question: Why might an interval communicate more uncertainty than a single sample mean?

slides.title: A confidence interval form
slides.body: A two-sided mean interval is centered at the sample mean.
slides.question: If the mean is 12 and the margin of error is 1.5, what are its endpoints?

slides.title: Margin of error
slides.body: The margin of error is the distance from the point estimate to either endpoint of a symmetric confidence interval.
slides.question: For an interval from 10 to 14 minutes, what is the margin of error?

slides.title: Confidence level
slides.body: A 95% confidence procedure captures the fixed population parameter in about 95% of repeated intervals under its assumptions.
slides.question: What would 95% describe if we repeatedly sampled and constructed intervals?

slides.title: A repeated-sample view
slides.body: Imagine 100 independent random samples, each producing a 95% confidence interval using a valid procedure.
slides.question: Should exactly 95 of the intervals be guaranteed to contain μ?

slides.title: The two tails
slides.body: A central confidence level leaves the remaining normal area in two equal tails.
slides.question: For 95% confidence, how much area belongs in each tail?

slides.title: A critical z value
slides.body: The positive critical value z* cuts off α/2 in the upper standard-normal tail.
slides.question: Which area to the left identifies z* for 95% confidence?

slides.title: Finding the critical value
slides.body: For 95% confidence, the standard-normal critical value is approximately 1.96.
slides.question: What probability lies between -1.96 and 1.96?

slides.title: The known-SD method
slides.body: A z interval for μ uses a known population SD and a normal or adequately approximated sampling distribution of the mean.
slides.question: What would you check beyond sample size before choosing this method?

slides.title: Standard error for the interval
slides.body: Synthetic independent random sample: n=64, mean=12 minutes. The population is normal with known SD 4 minutes.
slides.question: What standard error belongs in the confidence interval?

slides.title: The mean margin of error
slides.body: For a known population SD, the mean margin of error is a critical value times standard error.
slides.question: For σ=4, n=64, and z*=1.96, what is EBM?

slides.title: Constructing a mean interval
slides.body: Synthetic independent random sample: n=64, mean=12 minutes. Normal population; known SD=4 minutes; 95% confidence; z*=1.96.
slides.question: What is the confidence interval for μ?

slides.title: Interpreting the interval
slides.body: Synthetic result: a 95% confidence interval for mean transfer duration is 11.02 to 12.98 minutes.
slides.question: How would you state this result about the population mean?

slides.title: A fixed parameter
slides.body: Synthetic result: one calculated 95% interval is 11.02 to 12.98 minutes. The population mean is fixed.
slides.question: Does the procedure assign a 95% probability to that fixed mean lying inside this particular interval?

slides.title: Mean versus individual values
slides.body: Synthetic result: a 95% confidence interval for μ is 11.02 to 12.98 minutes.
slides.question: Does this imply that 95% of individual transfer durations lie in the interval?

slides.title: Recovering the point estimate
slides.body: Synthetic result: a symmetric mean confidence interval is 18.4 to 21.6 seconds.
slides.question: What sample mean produced this interval?

slides.title: Recovering the margin
slides.body: Synthetic result: a symmetric mean confidence interval is 18.4 to 21.6 seconds.
slides.question: What is its margin of error?

slides.title: More confidence
slides.body: Use the same sample and known population SD. Compare 90% and 99% confidence intervals.
slides.question: Which interval is wider?

slides.title: More observations
slides.body: Model: population SD and confidence level remain fixed. Increase n from 64 to 256.
slides.question: How does the margin of error change?

slides.title: More population variation
slides.body: Keep sample size and confidence level fixed. Double the known population SD.
slides.question: How does the interval width change?

slides.title: Planning a sample size
slides.body: For known σ, a desired margin E determines a sample size, rounded upward.
slides.question: For σ=4, E=0.5, and z*=1.96, what n is needed?

slides.title: A precision target
slides.body: Model: a 95% mean interval has margin 1 minute at n=64, with known population SD.
slides.question: What sample size would target a margin of 0.5 minutes?

slides.title: Precision and bias
slides.body: A synthetic sample measures only successful transfers; failed transfers are excluded.
slides.question: Would increasing n make its confidence interval valid for all transfer attempts?

slides.title: A value inside the interval
slides.body: Synthetic result: a 95% interval for μ is 11.02 to 12.98 minutes. A claim states μ=12.
slides.question: Is the claimed value compatible with this interval?

title: A Single Population Mean using the Student t Distribution

slides.title: An unknown population SD
slides.body: When σ is unknown, a one-sample mean interval estimates it with the sample SD s and uses a t critical value.
slides.question: Does a large sample make the population SD known?

slides.title: An estimated standard error
slides.body: An estimated standard error for a sample mean uses s in place of σ.
slides.question: For s=5 minutes and n=25, what is the estimated standard error?

slides.title: A t statistic
slides.body: A t statistic standardizes a sample mean using its estimated standard error.
slides.question: What extra estimated quantity distinguishes this from the known-SD z statistic?

slides.title: The t distribution
slides.body: A Student t distribution is symmetric about zero and has heavier tails than the standard normal.
slides.question: What additional uncertainty might those heavier tails reflect?

slides.title: Degrees of freedom
slides.body: For a one-sample t procedure, the degrees of freedom are n-1.
slides.question: What degrees of freedom belong to a sample of 25 observations?

slides.title: Why n-1?
slides.body: For a sample mean, the deviations from that mean sum to zero.
slides.question: If four of five deviations are known, can the fifth vary freely?

slides.title: Changing degrees of freedom
slides.body: As degrees of freedom increase, the t distribution approaches the standard normal.
slides.question: Would df=4 or df=100 produce heavier tails?

slides.title: A critical t value
slides.body: A positive t* value cuts off α/2 in the upper tail of the appropriate t distribution.
slides.question: Which degrees of freedom and left-tail area locate t* for n=25 and 95% confidence?

slides.title: Comparing critical values
slides.body: Given: at 95% confidence and df=24, t*=2.064. The standard-normal value is z*=1.96.
slides.question: How would the two values affect margins computed with the same estimated standard error?

slides.title: Conditions for a t interval
slides.body: Use independent random observations and a normal population, or a sample large enough for a reasonable approximation without problematic skewness or outliers.
slides.question: Why would a small sample with an extreme outlier deserve caution?

slides.title: A small normal sample
slides.body: Synthetic independent random sample: n=10 from a normal population with unknown σ.
slides.question: Is n<30 by itself a reason to reject the t method?

slides.title: A problematic small sample
slides.body: Synthetic random sample: n=8, strong right skew, and one value far above all the others.
slides.question: Would a t interval automatically be reliable?

slides.title: Checking independence
slides.body: A synthetic sample contains 25 consecutive measurements from one machine whose output drifts over time.
slides.question: What assumption needs attention before using s/√n?

slides.title: Choosing z or t
slides.body: Synthetic independent random sample: n=100; the population SD is unknown and the sample SD is 5 minutes.
slides.question: Which method estimates μ: known-SD z or one-sample t?

slides.title: The t margin of error
slides.body: A one-sample t margin is its critical value times the estimated standard error.
slides.question: For t*=2.064, s=5, and n=25, what is EBM?

slides.title: Constructing a t interval
slides.body: Synthetic independent random sample: n=25, mean=12 minutes, s=5 minutes. Normal population; unknown σ; 95% confidence; t*=2.064.
slides.question: What is the confidence interval for μ?

slides.title: Interpreting a t interval
slides.body: Synthetic result: a 95% t interval for mean processing time is 9.94 to 14.06 minutes.
slides.question: What population quantity does this interval estimate?

slides.title: Individual spread and mean precision
slides.body: Synthetic sample: n=25, sample SD=5 minutes, estimated standard error=1 minute.
slides.question: Which number describes spread among observed processing times?

slides.title: A higher confidence level
slides.body: Use the same sample, s, and degrees of freedom. Compare 95% and 99% t intervals.
slides.question: What changes in the interval formula?

slides.title: A larger sample
slides.body: Hold the observed mean, sample SD, and confidence level fixed while n increases.
slides.question: How do standard error and the critical t value each respond?

slides.title: A raw-data interval
slides.body: Synthetic independent random sample from a normal population, in seconds: 18, 19, 20, 21, 22. Unknown σ; 95% confidence; t*=2.776.
slides.question: What t interval for μ follows from these observations?

slides.title: Retaining units
slides.body: Synthetic sample mean and sample SD are both measured in seconds.
slides.question: What units should the standard error, margin of error, and interval endpoints have?

slides.title: The reported conclusion
slides.body: Synthetic result: a 95% t interval for μ is 9.94 to 14.06 minutes.
slides.question: Would this establish that the mean is exactly 12 minutes?

slides.title: An interval and a claim
slides.body: Synthetic result: a 95% t interval for μ is 9.94 to 14.06 minutes. A claim states μ=8.
slides.question: Is 8 minutes compatible with this interval?

slides.title: A population proportion
slides.body: A population proportion p is the fraction of population members with a specified outcome.
slides.question: What outcome would define p when studying use of a campus printing service?

slides.title: A sample proportion
slides.body: The sample proportion is the number of observed successes divided by the sample size.
slides.question: For 128 successes among 400 observations, what is the sample proportion?

slides.title: Two notation choices
slides.body: This textbook uses p′ for the sample proportion; p̂ denotes the same statistic.
slides.question: Which symbol refers to the unknown population proportion?

slides.title: Count or proportion?
slides.body: Synthetic random sample: 128 of 400 students used the printing service this week.
slides.question: Which number is a success count, and which number is the sample proportion?

slides.title: A binary outcome
slides.body: A proportion records whether each observation meets a specified condition.
slides.question: Would average pages printed per student be a proportion problem?

slides.title: Sampling variability of proportions
slides.body: For independent binary observations with success probability p, the sample proportion has mean p and SD √(p(1-p)/n).
slides.question: What happens to this SD when n quadruples?

slides.title: An estimated standard error
slides.body: A proportion interval estimates the standard error by replacing unknown p with the observed sample proportion.
slides.question: For p̂=0.32 and n=400, what is the estimated standard error?

slides.title: Successes and failures
slides.body: The textbook requires more than five observed successes and more than five observed failures for its ordinary normal-approximation proportion interval.
slides.question: Does a synthetic sample with 128 successes and 272 failures pass this check?

slides.title: A sparse success sample
slides.body: Synthetic random sample: 2 successes and 38 failures.
slides.question: Would a normal-approximation proportion interval meet the success-failure check?

slides.title: Independence for proportions
slides.body: Random sampling supports representativeness; independence also matters for the standard error formula.
slides.question: Would surveying every member of a few randomly selected clubs automatically give independent responses?

slides.title: A sample fraction
slides.body: For sampling without replacement, n≤10% of the population is a common independence approximation.
slides.question: Would a sample of 400 from 20,000 students meet that guideline?

slides.title: A proportion margin of error
slides.body: A normal-approximation proportion margin is a critical z value times estimated standard error.
slides.question: For p̂=0.32, n=400, and z*=1.96, what is EBP?

slides.title: Constructing a proportion interval
slides.body: Synthetic independent random sample: 128 of 400 students used printing this week. The population is large; use 95% confidence and z*=1.96.
slides.question: What is the normal-approximation confidence interval for p?

slides.title: Interpreting a proportion interval
slides.body: Synthetic result: a 95% interval for printing-service use is 0.274 to 0.366.
slides.question: How would you state this interval in percentages for the population?

slides.title: Percentage points
slides.body: Synthetic result: an estimated proportion is 32%, with margin of error 4.6 percentage points.
slides.question: What are the percentage endpoints?

slides.title: Confidence is about a procedure
slides.body: A valid 95% proportion interval procedure captures the fixed p in about 95% of repeated intervals.
slides.question: Does 95% mean that 95% of students use the printing service?

slides.title: The plus-four adjustment
slides.body: A plus-four interval uses two added successes and two added failures in its adjusted proportion.
slides.question: For a synthetic sample with 8 successes among 40 observations, what is the adjusted proportion?

slides.title: When to use plus four
slides.body: The textbook recommends plus four when confidence is at least 90% and the sample size is at least 10.
slides.question: Would a sample of 24 observations at 85% confidence meet these recommendations?

slides.title: A plus-four interval
slides.body: Synthetic independent random sample: 8 of 40 students used printing this week. Large population; 95% confidence; z*=1.96.
slides.question: What plus-four confidence interval for p follows?

slides.title: Changing confidence
slides.body: Use the same observed sample proportion and sample size. Compare 90% and 99% confidence intervals.
slides.question: Which margin of error is larger?

slides.title: Changing sample size
slides.body: Hold the observed proportion and confidence level fixed. Increase n from 400 to 1,600.
slides.question: How does the estimated margin of error change?

slides.title: Planning a proportion sample
slides.body: A planning estimate p₀ gives a sample-size formula, rounded upward, for a desired margin E.
slides.question: For p₀=0.32, E=0.03, and z*=1.96, what n is needed?

slides.title: Planning without an estimate
slides.body: When no planning estimate is available, p₀=0.5 gives the largest value of p₀(1-p₀).
slides.question: Why would this choice be conservative for planning sample size?

slides.title: A conservative planning problem
slides.body: Plan a 95% proportion interval with margin at most 0.03. No prior proportion estimate is available; use z*=1.96.
slides.question: What sample size should be planned?

slides.title: Precision cannot remove bias
slides.body: Synthetic online poll: 90% of 5,000 voluntary respondents favor longer library hours.
slides.question: Would its small calculated margin of error establish representativeness of all students?

slides.title: A claim and an interval
slides.body: Synthetic result: a 95% interval for printing-service use is 0.274 to 0.366. A claim states p=0.50.
slides.question: Is the claimed proportion compatible with this interval?

slides.title: Estimate versus null model
slides.body: For a proportion interval, standard error uses p̂. A proportion test may instead use a hypothesized p₀.
slides.question: Why could two analyses of the same sample use different standard errors?
